speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43 I desire to present a motion concerning a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Imperial Oil Company Limited has increased the price of crude oil by 25 cents a barrel effective May 1. This and other recent increases have no relation to increased costs of production and are related entirely to the oil shortage in the United States of which the oil companies are taking an unfair advantage.
In view of the fact that the area west of the Ottawa Valley has been made a captive market for western oil by act of parliament and that consumers are entitled to protection from unjustified increases in the price of crude oil and gasoline, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding):
That the government take immediate steps to introduce legislation empowering the National Energy Board to set fair and equitable prices for all crude oil produced and sold in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. James Gillies (Don Valley) (for Mr. Baldwin) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
That this House deplores the failure of the government to take concrete and effective action against the rising cost of living, so evident in the price of shelter, food and clothing; and therefore urges the government to impose an immediate temporary freeze so as to enable it to develop a satisfactory plan in conjunction with the provinces, industry and labour for the purpose of keeping the cost of living within acceptable limits.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this motion with the feeling that we are talking about one of the most important problems that is before the Canadian public today, the problem of the high cost of living and what we are going to do about it. It would seem to me that we do not have to debate the subject at length to ascertain that we have a serious inflationary problem in Canada. The consumer price index has increased by 6.6 per cent and the food component of that index has increased 12.9 per cent. All the forecasts we have indicate that inflation is going to be with us in the future. I know that these forecasts can be very difficult. Certainly, the forecast made a year ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in his budget, when he hoped that there would be reasonable price stability during this year, has not come true. I mention that not in a pejorative sense at all, but merely recognizing how difficult it is to make good forecasts in this particular area. I accept the explanation given by the Minister of Finance and the government many times that there have been great difficulties throughout the world in terms of food supplies, rising incomes and the rising expectations of people who are using more food. I accept those statements and would not debate them here today.
What I should like to debate is how we are going to evolve ways to deal with these particular problems in this country, and what we should do about inflation and our monetary and fiscal policy in a general sense. There are those who would argue that we should live with inflation as it is. A conventional part of economic wisdom says that inflation and full employment must go together, that we should go for full employment and be willing to live with the inflation it generates. I think that is a defeatist attitude, a program that is basically unacceptable in any contemporary economy, in any contemporary country. The inflation that could be experienced in a country such as Canada could be so high that we could not expect the Canadian people to bear such an unjust burden. People on fixed incomes are desperately burdened as it is. Those planning a pension or insurance program are already badly hit by inflation. Certainly, the great regional disparities in this country mean that the burdens of inflation fall heaviest on those who live in areas of low income.
We have unleashed in Canada today a series of expectations which bode ill for us in the future. Historically, many countries have found themselves in serious economic difficulties in terms of employment and economic growth because of unbridled inflation. So, we must do something about those inflationary forces in the Canadian economy at this time.
But beside that, and apart from that, the fact that we are experiencing a cycle of inflation in Canada today indicates, I think, that we have not come to grips with the problems of economic management in the Canadian economy. In the last two or three years we have had an inordinate level of unemployment. Our level of unemployment has been among the highest of any industrialized country in the world and we all applaud the reduction of this high level, even by a slight amount. There has been an enormous underutilization of our productive resources, and we have probably lost between $5 billion and $6 billion of
May 10, 1973

possible production per year because the economy has been operating below capacity.
The same can be said of taxes. We have lost a great amount of tax income which would have been generated by people who would have been working. We have had an economic policy that, very simply, has led to an increasing proportion of foreign control of our own economy. We have operated under an economic policy which simply has not worked for Canada and the amount of inflation from which we now suffer simply underlines this fundamental fact.
What worries the people of Canada and must worry all in the Parliament of Canada is this: As we enter this pattern of upswing and inflation, are we entering into the classical cycle when price expansion will eventually cause economic contraction? Will there be once again lost production, and are we, going to experience a classical business cycle? Analysts are saying that the high costs of today will be reflected in higher costs tomorrow which means there will be more inflation. The situation certainly calls for action right away.
Why are we experiencing the present level of inflation in Canada? There are two major causes of inflation. The first well known cause is cost-push, the cause or the inflation which we experienced last year, a matter which appeared to be a matter of great concern to those responsible for economic policy at that time. They asked, how is it possible that we have both inflation and high unemployment? The answer is, of course, that the inflation was not related to demand factors at all. There was cost-push inflation operating in Canada during the last two or three years, and that cost-push inflation should have been dealt with then. So, we were in the ignominious position of having a high level of unemployment and high levels of inflation.
What has happened now, and the reason that we have such great problems in Canada today, is that the cost-push inflation generated two or three years ago has now been supplemented by demand-pull inflation. Actually, we have both, and because we suffer from both forms, we must simply do something about it. Why has demand-pull inflation come about? One could argue that it has come about because incomes are rising. However, basically and primarily, demand-pull inflation, as we are today experiencing it, has come about as a result of the futile attempt of dealing with the inflationary problems of three years ago, as if it were caused by demand-pull and therefore by introducing high interest rate policies, a slowdown of the economy, and fiscal policies which stopped normal growth. So, we have shortages of supply now. The occurrence of cost-push inflation and demand-pull inflation together are creating inflationary expectations in the economy which the economy simply cannot sustain.
The real question is not necessarily why do we have this inflation, but what can we do about it? What kind of policy can we evolve that will make it possible for Canadians to have reasonably full employment and price stability at the same time? How can we cope with the situation in which the Canadian economy now finds itself? No one would argue, I least of all, that this question can be solved in any simple fashion. At the same time, it appears to me
Increased Cost of Living
that there are basically three approaches that can be taken to solve this particular problem.
The first is the great, classical approach, the traditional approach, which says that if there is inflation in the economy, you must slow down or dampen the economy, raise interest rates, impose high taxes and cut off excess purchasing power. This supposedly stops the forward movement of the economy and slows down the inflationary spiral. That was the policy followed by the government in 1970 and that is the policy that some of us are frightened the government will follow again. That policy, of course, will not work. It will not stop inflation unless you generate unacceptably high levels of unemployment. We are still suffering from the use of such a policy three years ago. One can give the government great credit for bringing the rate of inflation in Canada down to quite low levels through such a policy. However, in doing so, it paid a cost that was enormously high, a cost Canadians today are not prepared to pay again and inflation was only temporarily checked.
The question one must ask is, why does that classical approach not work now? Why did we end up having high unemployment and inflation at the same time, even though there was a slow down in the economy? The reason the policy does not work is that such a policy is designed to work in an economy which is totally competitive, where competitive forces are operating all the time. The trial of that policy two or three years ago, made it self-evident that the Canadian economy had within it a series of blocks, of power groups which do not respond the way competitive markets do. We do not have perfectly competitive economy. So, we find that the traditional policy for fighting inflation does not work. The Phillips curve that people talk about is not applicable. We do not have acceptable trade-offs between employment and inflation. Consequently, it does not make good sense to follow the traditional policy.
The second thing I wish to say about that policy is that it depends upon enormously good economic forecasting and analysis. I have argued many times in this House that we are not properly organized in Canada for economic policy making. We need a system of competent economic forecasting, but do not have it. I do not want to press that point except to say that if we are to use monetary and fiscal policies alone to create full employment and combat inflation, we must be very sure that we are accurately measuring the leads and lags that take place in the economy. Our estimation and analysis in this country of these leads and lags has been very poor indeed. We just have not been able to predict them. Whether anybody else could do so I am not prepared to say, but the government has not been able to do so. Relying on a policy when we do not have the tools to undertake it is folly indeed. We know that if you follow the classical way to fight inflation in this country, the policy is not going to work. It has not worked in the past and will not work in future, and we must reject the idea that it will.
I do not think anybody in this parliament is prepared to see the Bank of Canada tighten the money supply and raise interest rates to slow down production in order to get inflation under control. That is a perfectly unacceptable way to approach this problem at the present time.

On the other hand, if we do not follow the traditional method, we must do something else. We are not prepared, it seems to me, to accept the rate of inflation prevalent in the economy. It affects expectations involving, among other things, international trade. If we cannot accept it, one must ask, what are the alternatives?
One alternative is calling for voluntary restraints, asking everyone not to raise prices, asking labour not to raise wages and industrialists not to sell labour not to raise wages and industrialists not to sell their goods at higher prices. This was attempted but did not work. The thrust was made, but did not work. What is left?
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that, given the structure of the economy and the problems we are facing, we simply have to come to some sort of enforced incomes policy if we are to get rid of the inflation which is doing so much harm to so many Canadians at the present time. Nobody really approaches such a solution to the inflationary problem with any pleasure. I agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) that you have to approach the idea of making the policy work with care. However, I and the members on my side of the House, at least, feel strongly that we must do something to contain inflation. The people of Canada, I think, feel the same way. I think the people of Canada are looking for somebody to give leadership in this area and say, "Let us try this, let us make the economy work effectively."
What are the arguments against an incomes policy? What are the arguments why we should not attempt to adopt incomes policy? The first argument is that it will not work. I reject that out of hand. There is no reason to believe we cannot design an incomes policy in this country that will work. One looks at the experience of other countries, particularly the United States and England and it is clear that the record is mixed.
Indications from the British experience are not in, although we know the inflationary rate in that country has been reduced. One has to be careful of international comparisons, but I believe the rate has dropped roughly from 10 per cent to 6 per cent. We know that until they went to phase three in the United States, the American experience worked well. When they went to phase three, it worked badly. I reject out of hand the idea that we are incapable of designing in this country an incomes policy that will work. All we need to have is the will, the courage and the leadership to put it into effect.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
The second reason it is said we should not have a policy is that it would create a vast bureaucracy to administer the program. No one is talking about an incomes policy today that is comparable to the incomes policy operated in the forties during the war. It is a different situation altogether. Nobody is talking about rationing. We are talking about an incomes policy with no rationing. We could administer and operate an incomes policy in this country with something in the neighbourhood of 800 to 1,000 people. What the figure would actually be, I would not suggest specifically, but we know that when the United States with 225 million people ran its

income policy, they ran it with 1,200 people. The argument put forward that we would have a vast bureaucracy does not wash in the present situation.
The third reason that is given for not having an incomes policy in Canada is that we have an open economy. It is said that any country where 25 per cent of the gross national product is generated through international trade cannot make an incomes policy work. Again, it creates some difficulties. My own view is that they are far from insurmountable. Indeed, it would not be a bad idea to look more carefully at our export and import policies at this time, as well as our capital flow problems, and relate them to a growth program in Canada.
Finally, it is argued it would not work because the people are not ready for it and do not want it. What evidence is there? Every Gallup poll you look at, and I do not like to mention Gallup polls, indicates the Canadian people want some sort of incomes policy in this country at the present time. Certainly, most members of parliament found during the Easter recess that the major problem facing Canada today is the cost of living. There is no question about it. How long do Canadians have to wait before some action is taken to deal with this p; oblem? The Canadian people are willing, able and eager to have positive approach taken to lower the cost of living. These are the arguments made against it.
What are the arguments for it? Certainly, the argument of getting the cost of living under control is important. The field of housing, which will be dealt with later, is terribly important. With the rate of inflation today only 6 per cent of the families in Toronto can afford to buy a single family home if they are not to spend more than two and one half times their income on housing. The present rate of inflation in the cost of housing today, if compounded, and I know these figures have been quoted before, means that in the year 2,000 the average selling price of a single family house in Toronto would be $250,000, a quarter of a million dollars. We have to break such inflationary expectations.
An incomes policy would give us time to work out economic policies that would lead to the proper use of our resources, a stable employment program, a stable import-export program, a program that would allow the Canadian economy to move forward the way in which it should. I cannot state how sincerely our party is committed to the fact that now in Canada we should have a 90 day freeze on incomes, prices, rents and dividends as a start in attacking the inflation problem in the Canadian economy.
I want to make it very clear that we think that the 90 day period of time should be used, and in this I agree completely with the leader of the New Democratic Party, to consult with the provinces, leaders of labour, the leaders of industry, leaders of agriculture and leaders of consumer groups to work out a stabilization program. It has never been part of the Conservative party policy to have a 90 day freeze and that's it. We believe an incomes policy has to be an integral part of our monetary and fiscal policy if this country is going to operate with full employment and reasonably stable prices.
We would use the 90 days to develop the program in detail. We think guidelines should be developed for measuring acceptable changes in prices and incomes. We sug-
May 10, 1973

gest guidelines that are not voluntary, but that are enforceable. When there are productivity changes, these can be taken into account and remedies can be provided for those suffering inequitably because of the program. There is no reason why it cannot be done. We believe it can and should be done. In this economy, we have had enough experience in the old fashioned idea of monetary theory alone and fiscal policy alone, fighting inflation and bringing about full employment. It is not working. How much evidence do we need? We think it is essential to supplement monetary and fiscal policies with an incomes policy right now.
Before 1936, before Lord Keyne's great work, anyone who suggested there were times a government had a responsibility of operating without a balanced budget in order to get full employment was totally rejected. Surely, in the seventies we are not so blind that we are going to allow the Canadian people to be damaged by inflation and accept high levels of unemployment because we are unwilling to concede the proposition that it may be necessary now to supplement traditional policies with an incomes policy.
In this parliament, there has been debate after debate of all kinds of what are responsibilities of government. But surely, no one can argue against the proposition that it is a central responsibility of the federal government to follow policies to provide full employment and price stability. Surely this cannot be argued. It must be the central thrust, the central responsibility of the federal government. This is a responsibility which the government is not accepting, and I hope hon. members on the treasury benches opposite will accept our suggestion, will adopt an incomes policy, relate it to monetary and fiscal policy and get this country moving again.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we address ourselves to this motion with a recognition that rising prices in this country involve us all in a matter of growing concern-a concern felt by the country as a whole and shared by this House. No one is going to deny that inflation is hurting every Canadian. I must say the government is watching the situation with a commitment to do everything it can to ensure that low income families, in particular, are left with sufficient disposable income to cope with the rise in prices. The economic responses are not easy.
I listened with great care to the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) and I still do not know what economic responses he would make in sufficient detail to allow a considered judgment to be made upon them. I want to suggest to him that there are no magic, clear-cut solutions and it is no use deluding ourselves or the country into believing that a solution is easy. I do not believe posturing is going to provide a solution, nor will rhetoric, nor political cosmetics.

I continue. This is the Leader of the Opposition speaking:
It is important for us to recognize the far-reaching implications of such controls which, by their very nature, could be nothing better than a short-term solution taken as a final resort after all other means had failed.
They would cause untold resentment among groups and individuals who felt unfairly done by and they would result in a climate of constant confrontation. In additon, of course, they would inevitably lead to a highly centralized and therefore inefficient form of economic planning.
I say as strongly as I can that we must make a further, serious effort at a time when inflation is partially, if temporarily under control. This is the time to act again to set up a pattern for co-operation. And this must be combined with monetary and fiscal policies which will appear credible and workable to the people involved.
I agree with the last few words of that citation. I am sure the knowledgeable members of this House-and by definition every member of this House is knowledgeable on these matters-will recognize the problem of inflation is worldwide in origin. There is no way in which a major international trading nation like Canada can insulate itself from these forces. To suggest that it can do so represents a flagrant attempt to mislead the Canadian people. I say to the hon. member for Don Valley that if this recently-acquired obsession with controls, for whatever motives he might care to have attributed to him-maybe the word "obsession" is a little too strong-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: -is based only on the fact that we ought to have wage and price controls in this country in order to give it a try, run it up the flagpole and see if anyone salutes it, to use the old Walter J. Thompson aphorism, then surely he is deluding himself, the House and the people.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman was talking about inflationary expectations. I venture to say him that every time he brings up this matter in the House in these terms he is prompting expectations that if he were in power-fortunately this is an academic question-it would result in a self-fulfilling prophecy and prices would be escalated even more than they have been escalating. I suggest to him that this is a self-defeating type of policy.
Let us analyse the underlying situation. While Canada's price performance has been significantly better than that of most other industrial nations, it has felt the impact of the global increase in food prices and the price of commodities. When I talk of commodities I am talking of international commodities such as wool and cotton which affect our clothing prices. Recent figures published by Statistics Canada indicate that as a result of my budgetary measures the cost of children's clothing did not rise following the relief granted from sales tax. If you look at the figures relating to international commodity prices of lumber, which of course affects the cost of housing, you will see there are world-wide shortages. These increased prices result from adverse weather conditions, failure of world crops or a general increase in world-wide demand- for example, in an affluent country such as Japan, which is becoming more consumer oriented-flowing from a sharp upturn in economic growth as well as an increase in personal incomes. This is a situation that we must recognize. Our economy is vulnerable because we handle large amounts of imports and exports and we are not immune from the contagion of this world-wide problem.
Aside from food, let us look at wages and salaries and other commodities. These have been rising, but they have been rising relatively stably. When I take a close look at what the Conservative party is proposing here, I come to certain conclusions, and they are these. The Conservative party is advocating an immediate temporary freeze. But they do not tell us what is to be frozen.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
If hon. members read carefully what the hon. gentleman opposite said today, they will find it impossible to distinguish whether he is talking about a temporary freeze or continuing permanent controls. I invite hon. members to read the exact words that the hon. member used this afternoon. The motion then goes on to refer to developing-
-a satisfactory plan in conjunction with the provinces, industry

and labour for the purpose of keeping the cost of living within acceptable limits.
Again I ask, what do they propose to freeze? In an earlier motion which was put forward by the hon. gentleman's deskmate, the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), they proposed a freeze on food prices, except those at the farm gate. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whom do they think they are fooling? It should be obvious to any aduit Canadian, and certainly to every farmer, that if food prices are frozen at every level in our marketing system except at the farm gate, prices paid to the farmer for his output will be effectively frozen as well.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: No one says anything different.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Let me go on further. The farm gate is the point where most of the upward pressure has originated on food prices because of a shortage of supply to meet demand. Last year increases in the price of meat, fish, poultry, fruits and vegetables at the farm gate accounted for more than 60 per cent of the increase in food prices.
The effective freeze on food prices at the farm gate proposed by the official opposition, the Conservative party, would cause farmers to cut back on domestic production rather than encourage the essential increase in supplies which is sought by the government, and will eventually lead to a renewed price explosion. What hon. gentlemen opposite fail to realize is that the problem of food prices is one of shortage of supply. You do not curb the problem by imposing price controls; you only curb it by encouraging supply, and, as I say, the hon. member has failed to realize this.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Who wrote this speech?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Again I suggest to the House that it is impossible to apply a freeze or controls to imported goods. Imported goods in 1972 amounted to $1.2 billion and accounted for some 10 per cent of all food consumed in Canada. I submit it is also impossible to apply a freeze or controls to other imported goods. Last year total imports amounted to $18.5 billion, a substantial proportion of all goods purchased by Canadians.
If there is any doubt intellectually about the fact that the Conservative party proposal could hurt rather than help Canadians at this stage, it should be dispelled by a recent letter dated April 24, 1973 to the Wall Street Journal by John Kenneth Galbraith, a distinguished Canadian-born economist, a man who, as hon. gentlemen know, is one of the leading advocates in the United States of selective income controls of a permanent nature. As an exponent of controls, Galbraith wrote to take strong exception to action by the United States administration in imposing a freeze on meat prices. This is what he said, and I want to quote him:
The purpose of control is to arrest the interaction of wages on prices and prices on wages in that part of the economy characterized by strong unions. As such, it is an essential supplement to fiscal and, in its more limited role, monetary policy. It is nowise a substitute for such action. Controls should not be used where price increases are caused by an excess in aggregate demand or a shortage in the specific supply. If so used, some momentary effects
Increased Cost of Living
apart, the result will be either random shortages in the retail stores, violations or, more likely, both.
The present behaviour of meat prices, as of numerous other prices, shows every indication of being caused not by wage and cost increases but by the pull of demand. For this the right remedy is to stop playing games with the Congress over who will be responsible for the next tax increase. The need, whatever the prospective level of spending, is now for a prompt increase in taxes.
Not only do the Conservatives propose to compound problems in Canada by imposing a freeze on prices of food and other goods; they also propose to intensify these problems by vastly increasing fiscal and monetary stimulus. If there is one thing that even a student in first year economics should know, it is that if one is to attempt to apply any wage or income or prices policy, one has to have an accommodating fiscal and monetary policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Certainly; I agree with that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman agrees. When I presented my budget on February 19 and said that, evaluating the system as best I could, the maximum cash requirements of the government of Canada against the markets of Canada, weighing the problem of unemployment and the rising cost of living, was $2 billion, the hon. gentleman and his friend, the hon. member for Edmonton West, as well as their leader, said that that stimulus was only half as much as it should be, that we should double the deficit from $2 billion to $4 billion. Now, Mr. Speaker, these hon. gentlemen cannot have it both ways. They cannot ask for a policy that will restrain the rise in prices in this country by putting a lid on the economy of this country, and at the same time propose to juice up the fiscal element in the country by twice as much. I think on the basis of better judgment, the hon. gentlemen opposite might well want to reconsider the position they took about two months ago.
I do not think it is difficult for Canadians to understand the consequences of the proposal made by the Conservative party to put fire under the kettle and then increase the pressure of the burners, increasing economic stimulus and hoping that, by holding the lid on, they will prevent the lid from blowing off and a lot of water spilling over. The hon. gentleman is suggesting the imposition of a lid on our price structure in this country, and is in no way suggesting there should be an accommodating fiscal and monetary policy to go with it. I say that such a proposal is absolutely ridiculous.

speechtext: You are antediluvian.

The government does not contemplate the adoption of controls under current circumstances. We are only prepared to adopt them if, on balance, controls are supported by conclusive evidence that there would be net benefit to Canadians. We do not believe under the present circumstances that that will be the case.
We can recall the situation in the United Kingdom which faced a critical emergency situation with a rampant increase in prices and wages far exceeding that of most other industrial nations. We pointed out, and I repeat now,

May 10, 1973

that the United Kingdom exempted food at the farm gate. They also exempted imports from the freeze the subsequent controls.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: And look at what has happened in the U.K.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
We have had an even more vulnerable economy. The United States imposed a freeze followed by a control program in August of 1971 to deal with serious domestic and international economic problems of a kind that did not confront Canada. Why was the United States position different from ours? I suggest it was different because their dollar was in deep trouble and their trade figures showed a deficit position with a $10 million deficit on visible and invisible accounts.
While the United States program had some temporary success in curbing inflation, more recently U.S. prices have been increasing more rapidly than in Canada. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen to say that phase one and phase two worked, but a system of prices and incomes control has to be looked at over the entire phase of putting them on and how you are going to be able to take them off. I suggest to the House that these are the effects that have to be looked at.
In March the United States consumer price index was up 8.8 per cent over December, at seasonally adjusted annual rates, compared with 7.7 per cent at seasonally adjusted rates in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING

speechtext: Rising food costs were the major, and remain the major, cause of price pressures in the United States in recent months. What is of prime importance in the context of the present debate is the fact that U.S. food prices have soared despite the fact they continued under the more rigorous phase two control program and moved to phase three for most other prices in February. The increase at an adjusted annual rate in the U.S. for food prices, March over December, 16 per cent in Canada, compared to 29.8 per cent in the United States. In other words, despite the fact that there were price and wage controls in the United States for the first three months of this year, at annually adjusted rates the rise in food prices in the United States was double that of Canada.

Certainly, the Leader of the Opposition has had no success in persuading the heads of Conservative governments in Ontario, Alberta, New Brunswick and Newfoundland that a freeze-control program should be adopted. As a matter of fact, if the recent budget of his colleagues from Queen's Park can be taken into consideration, the 40 per cent rise in sales tax does nothing to relieve the inflationary pressures in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
The government's
policy, shown particularly by the February budget, is to restrain inflation by easing the pressure of rising prices on budgets of Canadian families through tax and tariff
May 10,1973

reductions which will increase take-home pay and moderate the cost of a wide range of consumer products, and will at the same time provide special relief for the elderly, the veterans and their families. In other words, the fundamental aim when there is that type of squeeze is to increase the disposable income of Canadians by tax reductions at the personal and sales tax level and to encourage an increase in supply by the agriculture industry, as well as by international competitive policy. That is the policy the government is currently following.
The real proof of the pudding can be found in a comparison of our costs with the disposable incomes of Canadians. I am concerned that the disposable incomes of Canadians, particularly for lower income Canadians, remains in a position to meet whatever increase there is in the cost of living. The aim of the budget and other government policies is to encourage an increase in supply of goods through an increase in production to meet rising demand; in other words, to deal with the basic source of the problem rather than to try to cover it up with a bandaid of the kind offered to Canadians by the Conservative party.
I want to recite again to the House the specifics of the last budget. They are reduced personal income taxes by the equivalent of 12 per cent to 13 per cent; raising the basic exemption from $1500 to $1600; ra sing the exemption for married couples from $2,850 to $3,000; cutting the basic federal tax by 5 per cent, providing a minimum reduction of at least $100 and a maximum of $500; indexing personal income taxes beginning in 1974; abolishing the federal sales tax on all children's clothing, footwear and wear-goods and non-alcoholic beverages and the special tax on toilet articles, cosmetics and clocks and watches with a manufacturer's price of less than $50; reducing tariffs temporarily by an average of five percentage points on a wide range of imported foods and other consumer goods totalling $1.4 million in 1972; permitting family farms to pass from one generation to another free of capital gains tax; removing restrictions for tax purposes on the reinvested earnings of small businesses; increasing the old age pensions to $100 a month effective April 1, 1973; raising the combined OAS/GIS to a maximum of $170 a month for single persons and $325 a month for couples; injecting a further $190 million into the economies of the slow-growth regions of Canada by including local school taxes on property in the calculation of equalization grants to the provinces. This represents 26 per cent of school taxes paid by the local ratepayers of the seven receiving provinces which, if it is passed along by the provinces to the local ratepayers, will increase their disposable incomes by that much.

I want to say that the policy of the government at this stage in our economic cycle is to increase the disposable income of Canadians, particularly those with fixed and lower incomes, and to increase the supply of agricultural and manufactured products by combined agricultural policies, tariff policies and fiscal and monetary policies. Our aim is to meet the problems with a sound economic policy and not by 90-day stop-gap measures; a sound economic policy that reflects the international forces applying in this phenomenon of domestic inflation that is apparent to most Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I begin my remarks, I want to say to my friends in the Conservative party that all of us listened very carefully and very courteously to the interesting speech of the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies). I noticed that while the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) was speaking, they did not return the same courtesy. I hope they will from now on. If the question of rising prices is as important as the hon. member for Don Valley said, and all of us agree, it seems to me this debate should be carried on with seriousness instead of in the way in which some members of this House have behaved during the past few minutes.
It occurred to me, as I watched the question period and the last few minutes in this House, that the members of the Conservative party think they can overcome the results of the Gallup poll by being negative, destructive and noisy. I want to tell them they cannot do that, Mr. Speaker.
I shall deal with the proposal of the hon. member for Don Valley in a moment, but I want to say to the Minister of Finance that it does not help to resolve the problem now before this House as well as before the people of Canada for him merely to recite again what he told us on February 19 and to make a speech which suggests that all that can be done has already been done, that nothing more should be done. I know of nothing less helpful to the situation in Canada than that kind of entirely unjustified complacent attitude which the Minister of Finance has shown. I could not help but notice when the hon. member for Don Valley spoke, that one of the reasons he gave that it is no longer possible to affect the price situation by creating unem-

May 10, 1973
Increased Cost of Living
ployment is that our economy is no longer competitive. That is what he said. I agree with him entirely. I merely find it very difficult to understand why he supports an economy that grows more and more monopolistic and therefore unable to deal with the real needs of the Canadian people. That is the basic difference between his very thoughtful approach to the problem and the approach which we of the New Democratic Party take.
He says blithely in his speech that countries have been hurt by inflation of this level. I do not know what decade he is talking about. If he is talking about the decade of the 1920's, there is no doubt he is right. But if he is talking about the decade of the 1960's and 1970's, I challenge him to give us an example of that kind of nonsense. Is he talking about Japan? Has its economy gone to pot? Is he talking about Germany? Has its economy gone to pot? Is he talking about any of the western European countries? The fact is, of course, that when you have rising prices throughout the world internationally-I am speaking now not from the point of view of Canadians who are hurt, and I will come back to that point in a moment, but from the point of view of the economy as an economy and from the view of our position internationally-and if the prices in your country are not rising at a level higher than the general situation your economy, in fact, is not hurt. Indeed, the fact is that Canada has not been hurt internationally. If that is the case, then what on earth is he talking about?
The Minister of Finance has already cited from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) a quotation which had been drawn to my attention earlier today, but let me say in general terms that the Leader of the Opposition and members of the Conservative party twitted the government for having a kind of paranoia about inflation, for being preoccupied with inflation and for being obsessed with inflation. The Conservative party spokesmen then were right because one can easily become obsessed with this question in the terms in which the hon. member for Don Valley spoke. The hon. member for Don Valley and the members of the Conservative party today are making precisely the same mistake. They are attempting to impose, if they had the opportunity, a freeze that is meaningless and undefined which would cause immense harm to a large part of the people of Canada, never mind the economy as a whole, and which would, in the first instance, be of particular harm to the farmers of this country.
I have said many times when addressing farm meetings, which I have had the pleasure of doing for many years, that I do not claim to be a farmer but I do claim to know a little about the situation in respect of our farm population in this country. For some three or four years, from about 1969 to 1972 inclusive, the farmers of this country, perhaps like the farmers in many other parts of the world but particularly in this country, were getting the raw end of the stick. Their prices were too low, their costs of production were rising all the time and they were being squeezed by international prices on the one hand which, they could not control, and on the other hand by the cost of production, which they could not control. Their income fell continually year by year. I say as one urban person in this country that if the consumers of Canada were paying higher prices for food only because the farmer was at least

getting a decent price for his products, the consumers of Canada would have no right to complain.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
This is were I part company with the Minister of Finance because my observation of the situation in Canada with regard to food prices and other prices, which I will come to in a moment, is that the purchaser in the supermarket and in other food stores does not pay a higher price now merely because the farmer is at last getting a decent price for his products. The consumer is also paying a higher price because of the monopolistic control of the food packaging, because of the waste in food advertising and packaging and because of the monopolistic control over the processing of food and the monopolistic control by the supermarkets in this country which gouge consumers beyond the point where it would be justified to raise prices because of the farmers' income.
I often go shopping with my wife. Time and time again she has drawn my attention to the fact that she picks a tin of something off the shelf which has a price and a label on it, that she then takes that label off and finds under it another price five cents lower and then takes that label off and finds a third price ten cents lower again. What that means is that the supermarket has had that tin on its shelf for months. It was brought in at a low price and the merchant is now taking advantage of the situation to get what the traffic will bear by gouging the housewife unnecessarily when she goes shopping. It is this kind of consideration that has made us demand a food prices review board and indeed a prices review board generally, if we could have one, because what you would have then would be an agency that would look into the reason for the increased prices; you would be able to expose the unfairness that exists. That is what we should be after. We should be able to expose the unjustifiable increase.
As I will suggest in a moment, Mr. Speaker, if the government took the necessary step, then somebody would have the authority to do something about the situation when prices have been unfairly raised. Everyone in this chamber, when he talks about inflation, is concerned, genuinely I believe- I do not for one moment question the integrity of the hon. member for Don Valley any more than I hope he questions mine-about the low income people in this country. There is one simple, decent, humane, moral way of dealing with that problem, and that is to raise the income of the low income people of this country-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING

To enter into a massive system of price, wage and incomes control

and I will come back to that in a moment-to enter into a massive system that will freeze injustices where they are and that will create divisions, and to suggest a 90 day freeze during which you can do nothing at all except wait for the whole thing to blow up when the 90 days are over, all in order to assist the low income people, is nonsense. The fact is that the old age pensioners, the families on welfare, and the people on low wages are now poor because our society has not been justly run, because the redistribution of wealth and
May 10, 1973

income stops at the gate of the Liberals and Conservatives, who are much more concerned with serving their corporate friends than with serving these people.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Of course, Mr. Speaker, I was glad to see the increase in the old age pension to $100 a month, but I say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and to the Minister of Finance that if they are concerned, as I know they are, about the condition of the old age pensioner, particularly in an era of rising prices and particularly when those rises are centered in food and shelter, then the way to deal with that is not to boast about an increase of only $13 and some odd cents above what the old age pension would have been, but to increase it much more, as could have been done, because the economy of Canada can well support it.
We supported the budget because it did have some income tax cuts on a very progressive basis for individual taxpayers, and we were glad to see that, but again I say that if we are concerned about the low income people one way to help is to increase their disposable income. There, I agree with the Minister of Finance. I merely disagree with him because the steps which are taken by governments, steps to increase this disposable income, are always puny steps, mincing steps, instead of adequate and humane steps to solve the problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: They help to solve the problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Sure, they do. If you increase the income of the low income groups, then of course you increase the demand for goods and services and so, at the same time, you have to increase supply.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: You have to have both.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Right. The point I am making is that instead of attempting an impossible and unfair system of price and wage controls, and it really is wages, not incomes, let us deal with the low income people in a way in which they can be dealt with justly and fairly and without harm to the economy.
I reject the idea of a freeze, not only because it is undefined but because it is a meaningless thing. I am not going to accuse the hon. member for Don Valley, as the minister did, that all he was suggesting was a freeze. I listened to the hon. member. I appreciate that what he said was, "Let us have a temporary freeze during which we will work out some policy of controls." I was interested when he said there was no reason why we could not have a system of controls that will work. He said we only need the will, the initiative and the leadership-all the things his party has not got, Mr. Speaker!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING

He said we only need these things to have a control system that will work. I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that I listened anxiously to him as I sipped a cup of coffee behind the curtain, to hear exactly what that price control system, what that income control system would be; where it would go, how long it would last, what the constitutionincreased Cost of Living
al problems are with the provinces, how those constitutional problems may be overcome, how long it will take to implement, what kind of bureaucracy will be required to enforce it. Will it apply to farmers, will it apply to wage earners, will it apply to wage increases that are already provided for in collective agreements, because there are such? What are the details of it, and indeed what are the broad outlines of it? And, Mr. Speaker, nary a single word on that from this ex-professor of economics who spoke so eloquently in other ways.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
The reason there was not a single word is not because the hon. gentleman is not intelligent and doesn't know economics. He is both; he is intelligent and knows economics, and because he knows economics he knows darn well there is no system of controls that has worked in the United States or Britain, or in any other part of the western world, or indeed even in the communist countries where, with all the totalitarian controls they have, they have not been able to do the kind of thing that the hon. member for Don Valley suggests is possible in Canada.
It is significant to note that when the Conservative party first started talking about this they talked about price and wage controls. They never talked about anything else but price and wage controls. Then, the hon. member for Don Valley joined their ranks. He is a much more tactful person, a little more sophisticated and thoughtful person. He saw it was unjust to control only wages, so he said, "Let us stop talking about price and wage control, and let us start talking about price and incomes control." Well, let me tell him, Mr. Speaker, that this is the kind of talk that the President of the United States engaged in, this great President of the United States whom the hon. member for Don Valley wants us to follow, not so far as Watergate, but up to the fence, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING

Let me inform the hon. member for Don Valley that if you compare the second quarter of 1971, the last full quarter before the Nixon economics were imposed, before the controls were imposed, with the fourth quarter of 1972, the latest full quarter on which I have information, we find that in the United States corporate profits before taxes increased 20.6 per cent, and corporate profits after taxes increased 25.1 per cent. It is true that dividends only increased 5.1 per cent, but undistributed profit increased 50.5 per cent. The profits were undistributed. The large corporations held in their coffers half as much again as the undistributed profits they had before the controls were imposed. Of what value is that to the people of the United States?
Remember there was an increase of 20.6 per cent for profits before taxes and 25.1 per cent for profits after taxes, but average straight time hourly earnings in manufacturing increased only 8.7 per cent on a seasonally adjusted basis. I would point out that the other figures I have given are also on a seasonally adjusted basis.
The reason I feel this talk about incomes control does not apply really to incomes can be put in the question:

Mr. Speaker, I say that the wages of organized workers are public knowledge, and if you want to know about an increase all you have to do is get hold of the union or the employers concerned. The wages of the unorganized worker can also be controlled because the government would have the greatest ally in that area, namely an employer who would rather pay less than more.
Those who talk about incomes control are not being entirely honest because they are talking about something that cannot be imposed. What can and would be imposed is control of working people in this country. There are too many working people in Canada making the minimum, and some below the minimum necessary for a decent living, for us to accept the idea of controlling their wages.
I have only two or three minutes left, Mr. Speaker, but I want to make one final point. It is this kind of consideration, the impossibility, the unworkability, the injustice- in fact, the senselessness-of temporary freezes, and the injustices and inequities of a system of control as well as the impossibility of doing it in peacetime that has made us support the idea of a food prices review board and a prices review board generally. If the prices which people have to pay are fair in relation to increased costs, then people just accept that and live with it, but I suggest there is a measure of unfairness in the increased prices and a prices review board could find that out.
Mr. Speaker, I draw your attention to the fact that Imperial Oil, followed by Shell and Gulf, increased the price of crude oil. Imperial Oil increased it on May 1 by 25

cents a barrel; that is a total of 55 cents a barrel since November, just six months, or a 20 per cent increase in the price of crude. Already that increase in the price of crude is being reflected in the increased price of gasoline to car owners. Again, this affects the farmers of Canada because the agricultural industry-although some members of this House may not know it-is the largest user of oil and energy in this country, as an industry. Pretty soon this increase imposed by Imperial and Shell and Gulf will be reflected in increased food prices because farmers' costs will increase as a result of it. Why were these prices increased, Mr. Speaker? Do we not have enough oil in Canada? Was there an increase in the cost of producing the oil? Not at all. They were increased in Canada because Imperial, Shell and Gulf can get a higher price outside this country. That is unfair to the people of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today is of great importance to the whole country, and hon. members. In fact, it says:
That this House deplores the failure of the government to take concrete and effective action against the rising cost of living, so evident in the price of shelter, food and clothing; and therefore urges the government to impose an immediate temporary freeze so as to enable it to develop a satisfactory plan in conjunction with the provinces, industry and labour for the purpose of keeping the cost of living within acceptable limits.
Mr. Speaker, the day before yesterday I believe, I asked the Prime Minister whether he would recommend the hospitalization of the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for the purposes of a psychiatric examination. The leader of the opposition was in the Maritimes at the

May 10, 1973

same time as I, some 10 days ago, and he promised that a Progressive Conservative government would improve the conditions over there by getting better prices for fish. He had also made the same promise to the western wheat growers and the dairy producers in Quebec. And upon his return to the House, he proposes freezing prices. This is completely incompatible!
Mr. Speaker, this matter, as I said earlier, is most important because it concerns Canadians. I would bet my shirt that tonight, on the CBC news, instead of reporting on this important item, they will talk about Viet Nam, as usual. They talk about the problems of foreign countries rather than Canadian problems; they forget to talk about our own problems-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE EFFECTIVE ACTION TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
It is not a Canadian problem. Our problem is the rising prices in Canada. By all means let us take an interest in what is going on the world, but let us begin by putting our own houses in order, including that of the member for Brome-Missisquoi.
Mr. Speaker,, in Canada we have provincial governments. In Quebec, we have a Liberal government, as in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. In Ontario, Alberta, New Brunswick and Newfoundland there are Progressive Conservative governments. In the three remaining provinces, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, there are New Democratic governments. Let us go and see if people are better off in those provinces, if prices are lower and if the cost of living is less than we know it to be in Ottawa, if we are to believe Canadian statistics.
Mr. Speaker, it is all very well to say: If I were in power, I would do this or I would do that. But the Progressive Conservatives were in power when inflation was growing in Canada. Why did they not fight it? Why did they not wipe it out? Why did they not take some action? Why did they not introduce legislation?
Mr. Speaker, it is all very well to say to the government: You have not done it right. But what would we do in their place? Even the spokesman for the Progressive Conservative party who spoke just now did not offer any solution. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said after that: There is no magic solution. So we have to put up with the present state of affairs, because there is no magic solution.
Mr. Speaker, the problem in Canada is not so much prices as the loss of our products. That is the real problem. Prime Minister Trudeau boasted recently that Canadian production would reach $102 billion for the first time in history, while the gross national income, including parliamentary allowances, everything included, would be about $70 billion. Now, I should just like hon. members to ask themselves: how and when can you buy $102 billion with $70 billion? That is a simple enough rule. How and when? Mr. Speaker, it is the system that tends to inflation, that leads us straight to inflation.
Increased Cost of Living
Not long ago Premier Bourassa of the province of Quebec went to the United States to borrow $100 million to finance part of the James Bay development, in the constituency of my colleague from Abitibi (Mr. Laprise); he managed to borrow this sum at 10 per cent interest for a period of 25 years. Here again, those who have done elementary mathematics can easily see that in 25 years we will be paying $250 million in interest alone, and that we will still owe the $100 million capital we borrowed.
Mr. Speaker, did the premier of the province come back from the United States with a cartload of American dollars? No: he came back with what is called a promissary note, a little piece of paper marked $100 million, 10 per cent interest, 25 years, signed Robert Bourassa, the whole thing endorsed by the entire population of Quebec province. So it all works by figures. What did the Americans base their $100 million on? On what they have? The Mis-sissipi, Watergate, Mr. Nixon's election? No! They based the $100 million on the feasibility of the James Bay project. If the project had not been good, Mr. Bourassa would not have got 25 cents from the United States. They studied the project and said: "All right, we will finance it".
Mr. Speaker, that is why we suggest using the Bank of Canada. The governor of that institution can write figures too. Based on what? Inflation? No; based on the James Bay project. He can do the same thing as the Americans. And then, we could lend to the provinces, and not just to Mr. Bourassa, without interest, as we so kindly do for India, Thailand, South America, countries of Europe, Africa, etc. They are interest-free loans for a period of 60 years. Recently a $48 million loan was granted.

An agreement to purchase Canadian products can be entered into in Winnipeg, in Quebec, in British Columbia. Obviously, we would not be purchasing all our material in Japan with those $100 million. Let us buy here, in Canada. There can be agreements between the provinces and the federal government. And the Bank of Canada is there for that purpose.
Mr. Speaker, they think that is funny. By the time India reimburses those interest-free $48 million loaned for 60 years, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will be 115 years old and he will no longer be around. As for little Justin, he will be barely 61. That is about the only change there will be.
Mr. Speaker, there is a solution to fight the current inflation: lower interest rates, make use of our financial institutions, become masters of our credit instead of going begging abroad. Do you think it is pleasant to see representatives of our municipalities going to Europe, to Switzerland, to Germany to borrow money for the development of our natural ressources? It is inconceivable that a government tolerates such a situation. As long as we continue in that direction and keep talking about price controls or control of whatever you want, this will lead to absolutely nothing.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance talked about a miraculous solution, but there is none. We have been

May 10, 1973
Increased Cost of Living
suggesting for quite a length of time that a compensated discount be granted at the retail level, following an agreement between a national commission and Canadian retailers whereby prices would not change. This would be an agreement not an imposition. Everyone is free to join or not. But if you join, then the government would order the payment of a 25 per cent compensated discount on retail prices, which means that for a $100 purchase the consumer would pay $75 and the government $25 as compensated discount to the retailer. The retailer would have $100 and inflation and price increases would thus be efficiently controlled. But no. Yesterday, the Prime Minister asked me whether that was constitutional or not; to my mind, he did not know whether the matter was constitutional or not. It seems to me we should look into it.
Indeed, I wonder what is keeping the Canadian parliament, which is sovereign, from passing a law to adopt a compensated discount, as was done anyway during the war in the case of milk.
Mr. Speaker, that is no miracle solution but a very normal one. Why does the government hesitate to try it out? What is it waiting for? Why speak of freezing prices which would lead right away to a black market? Why not try the solution advocated by the Social Credit party?
Mr. Speaker, I repeat: this is no miracle solution. The member for York South spoke of increasing the income of low wage earners. He is against price control. He has not always been against it, but now he is. I think that he has heard us often enough to reach this conclusion.
A price freeze is no good, really no good. They suggest increasing the income of workers, those who are drawing a small income. But how are we to increase this income? The hon. member has failed to explain. He has not referred to it.
I am going to tell you how. You must take from the haves and give to the have nots. That is the way to increase the income of the poor, that is the socialist solution.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian who earns $25,000, $50,000, $75,000 or $100,000 a year does not hide his money in a corner of his bedroom. He spends it, he buys things, he opens a business or something similar. His money is used for something, this is not saving. So, they are going to take it from him and give it to somebody who has less money. The total revenue remains exactly the same; the total national revenue will still amount to $70 billion and they will not be able to purchase the $32 billion worth of goods which are on the shelves, in stores, in wharehouses, in sheds, in back stores as we call them. To take from the rich to give to the poor will not solve anything.
The hon. member for York South stated that his solution would be wage control. This is exactly what I have just said. If you have the chance to make money, the government will watch you and take it away. Thus, private enterprise is killed, the stimulus which drives someone to do something. He is discouraged and then he says: If I have to work for the government, I will give up. This is what happens in private industry. So the solution of the New Democratic Party is not effective.
As far as we are concerned, we say that we should make up the difference between production and national income

at current prices, paying at first a compensated discount and then distributing a national dividend to every citizen. This is a solution.
Mr. Speaker, whatever may be said, whether it seems ridiculous or funny, as long as those solutions are rejected, we will continue to beat around the bush. We will always be considering absurd motions as the one introduced today and far-fetched solutions which do not solve anything but create worse problems.
Mr. Speaker, the Creditists are continuing to instil these principles into Canadians so that the products will be available to the Canadian people and allow them to be their own masters.

I am sure the minister will be participating in this debate. My time is limited. I am sure the minister will be able to ask all the questions he wants when I finish my speech. I am sure the minister hoped his announcement on his half-hearted attempt to meet the demands of the food prices committee and half-hearted attempt to meet the New Democratic Party half way would be obscured by the news flowing from this federal-provincial conference on welfare. That must surely be the explanation as to why the minister elected to make his statement at the time when the House was not sitting. Subsequent events have shown there was certainly no urgency.
The minister was trying to say he was treating this matter as one of great urgency. He could have at least waited one more week until parliament was in session and made his statement in the House, thereby allowing the members of this House to respond to the action the government was taking. But no, Mr. Speaker, the minister elected not to take that course. There is a good reason for that. The minister knew that the statement he made on April 27 setting up the prices review board would not be acceptable in this House and would not stand up to the scrutiny of this House. That is why he elected to make this statement when the House was not sitting. The committee recommended and I quote:
The Committee recommends:
1. That the Government give consideration to the advisability of introducing the necessary legislation to establish an independent Food Prices Review Board equipped with such powers as are
Increased Cost of Living
necessary to review prices, and that it report to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In its reports to the Minister, the Board could make recommendations concerning appropriate action to be taken.
The government does not intend to introduce legislation in this House. It does not intend to bring this review board into the House in any way, shape or form. Instead, they circumvent the House by using the provisions of the Inquiries Act to establish this commission. If the government had shown enough courage to meet the recommendations of the committee and to bring legislation before the House something might have been said for it, but the government knows full well it would have been faced with amendments and that these amendments would, at the very least, have had the effect of putting some teeth into the useless board whose establishment is proposed.
Given the situation in which parliament finds itself, the minister knows that the proposed review board, as announced by the minister on April 27, will not be acceptable and that hon. members would, by way of amendment, have considerably strengthened the board in fulfilment of their commitments and responsibilities. As a consequence, no legislation has been introduced. The board is to be set up under the Inquiries Act. What will it do? The provisions of the Inquiries Act will give the board no more power than could be exercised by the Special Committee on Trends in Food Prices. The commissioners will be able to call for papers and persons and examine witnesses. That was precisely the role of the special committee. Obviously there is no future for the special committee, because the special committee is now redundant by virtue of the minister's action.
But even allowing for all the limitations and shortcomings of the review board, surely there must be people in Canada who could be approached to serve on the board. Until yesterday not one Canadian had been approached. Nobody had been invited to participate in this work. No invitation had been extended to any Canadian asking him to chair this board. One wonders what has become of all the expertise which I am sure must be lying around in the bureaucracy of Ottawa left over from the Prices and Incomes Commission. One wonders, in particular, why Dr. Young was not called upon. After all, he must have amassed considerable experience during his tenure as chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission. I submit he was not consulted because, as a result of his experience, he has reached the conclusion that only some form of income control would effectively halt inflation in Canada. And this, as we all know, would prove embarrassing to the government.
There has been an adverse reaction across the country to the minister's statement. We know it is not acceptable to most of the consumer groups. I refer, for example, to a release by the Women Against Soaring Prices. In a brief dated May 2, this body expressed its views as follows:
Government guidelines for this Board are incomplete and unsatisfactory. Dependence upon "investigation and publicity" just is not powerful enough to deal with rising prices. Moral persuasion has not worked in the past and will not work in the future. At most, all that can be accomplished is a levelling-off effect on food prices.

That is the reaction of one group and it is re-echoed many times. I am sure the minister is aware of editorial opinion as expressed in the newspapers. The reaction of the editorial writers is consistent with the general reaction across the country. The minister's statement of April 27 was an affront to parliament. It showed contempt for this House and, more particularly, it was an affront to the special Committee on Trends in Food Prices which worked diligently to come up with the recommendations it placed before the House.
In the midst of all this, in the midst of the latest figures released by Statistics Canada a couple of days ago, showing a 2.6 per cent increase in the cost of food for the month of April, what are we doing? What is parliament doing? What are the priorities of the government? At a time when food, shelter and clothing prices are soaring, parliament occupies itself with amendments to the wildlife legislation. What are the legislative priorities for the balance of this week and next week? These open-ended opposition days, where the issue will not be resolved because there is no vote, by virtue of what I consider to be anomalies in the new rules, were designated by the government. And this at a time when the whole country was talking about the scandalous increase in the price of food.

That bill was withdrawn by the government because they were getting flak from the government of Quebec. That is true, and the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) knows of what I speak because he was the Prime Minister's emissary to Quebec. That was why the bill was withdrawn.

They talk about one man holding up third reading of that bill. The fact of the matter is that the House could have sat next day and given third reading to the measure. Or the government could have brought the bill on when the House met in emergency session in September to deal with the Vancouver dock strike. There was a disposition among all members to bring it on at that time.
The situation now is that after five years of study there is no FISP arrangement. It took approximately five years to come up with a Family Income Security Plan and now it is defunct. What do we have instead? We have a policy announced by the minister as a result of a federal-provincial conference under which the family allowance will be increased to $20. He talks about some new mechanism in connection with which he needs the consent of the provinces. I say to the minister: Bring in the increase in the present family allowances right away, as an interim measure. Let us not wait another six months for the new program mentioned by the minister following the federal-provincial conference. Let him bring in legislation now as a means of getting money directly into the hands of the low income group, those with large families and those living on fixed incomes, the people who are feeling the squeeze. The poor cannot wait six months for the minister's bill, they need money now. They have to buy food every day.
Where are the poor of this country? They are in the large cities where inflation is highest. They are in areas of regional disparity where incomes are low and unemployment is high. They constitue a very substantial majority in this country who are suffering from the consequences of the complete failure of the government to relieve the burden imposed on them by inflation. When the Prime Minister rises in this House to respond to questions, I challenge him to place the facts before the House instead of continuing to try to deceive the people of Canada. The fact is that we could have had the family income security plan, and we could have had it before the close of the last session of the last parliament; it could have been in effect now.
I point out that as an interim measure the government can change its legislative program and immediately bring in amendments to the present Family Allowances Act. There is a disposition on the part of members in the House to deal with this matter expeditiously because it would put money into the pockets of the poor, those with large families and on fixed incomes.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) spoke today, and I listened very carefully to what he said. I am sure that other members on the government side will confirm, and I am sure a reading of Hansard will also confirm, that the minister categorically rejected any suggestion of a freeze or any kind of controls as a means of fighting inflation. But I heard no reference whatsoever to what the government does propose to do. There was no mention in the minister's speech of the government's contingency plan. The fact is that there is no contingency plan.
